debrief.title: Replacement
text: COPY INTO sales_raw FROM the folder with FILEFORMAT = CSV, or Auto Loader with trigger(availableNow=True) and its own checkpoint, or a streaming table defined in SQL.
Add _metadata.file_name to bronze so every row says which file it came from.

debrief.title: Rebuilding
text: Recreate bronze from the files with the new load, then rerun silver and gold; check row counts per file against the source.

sayIt.question: Compare COPY INTO and Auto Loader for loading files into Delta tables.
points: Both load only new files: COPY INTO skips files it already loaded; Auto Loader tracks them in its checkpoint.
COPY INTO is a SQL command, retriable and idempotent.
Auto Loader is a Structured Streaming source (cloudFiles) that scales to billions of files.
Auto Loader adds schema inference, evolution and the rescued data column.
Databricks recommends streaming tables with Auto Loader for SQL users.

scenarios.title: Two streams, one checkpoint
scenarios.outcome: A copied notebook kept its checkpoint path, two queries fought over one table, and the proposed fix would have thrown away the record of what was processed.

content.bookmark: A checkpoint is one query's memory: what it read and what it committed. Never share one, and never delete one to make an error go away.

check.prompt: What does a Structured Streaming checkpoint store?
options: A full copy of the source data read so far, so it can be replayed
Offsets, commits, state and the query ID
Only the last row written
check.why: The checkpoint holds offsets (what each micro-batch read), commits (which batches reached the sink), state for stateful operations, and the query ID.

check.prompt: Two streams write one Delta table using the same checkpoint. Which error condition describes it?
options: DELTA_FILE_NOT_FOUND_DETAILED
TABLE_OR_VIEW_NOT_FOUND
DELTA_CONCURRENT_TRANSACTION
check.why: DELTA_CONCURRENT_TRANSACTION says several streams are using the same checkpoint to write the table. The fix is one checkpoint per query.

check.prompt: Which change to a streaming query generally needs a new checkpoint?
options: Changing the sink type
Changing the trigger interval
Adding a filter
check.why: Changing sources, stateful operations, the state schema or the sink type generally needs a new checkpoint; filters, rate limits and trigger intervals are generally safe.

check.prompt: How does the Delta sink avoid committing the same micro-batch twice after a restart?
options: It locks the table while writing
It compares every incoming row with the rows already in the table before it writes
It records each batch as a transaction identifier and skips one already committed
check.why: Transaction identifiers (an appId and version committed with the data) let the sink check whether a batch is already recorded and skip it: the mechanism behind exactly-once writes into Delta.

caseStudy.setting: A logistics company (fictional) streams parcel scans from a bronze Delta table into silver with a notebook job. To add a second feed of scans from a partner, an engineer copied the notebook, changed the source table, and left everything else, including the checkpointLocation, as it was.

events.what: Both jobs start. Within minutes one of them fails with DELTA_CONCURRENT_TRANSACTION; it retries and fails again.
A colleague suggests deleting the checkpoint folder "to clear the conflict" and starting both jobs again.
The team lead stops the change and asks what the checkpoint is for before anyone deletes it.

pipeline: bronze.scans and bronze.partner_scans · Delta tables, append-only
Two notebook jobs · same checkpointLocation /Volumes/ops/chk/scans_silver
silver.scans · Delta table, the shared target
tasks: What went wrong, and why would deleting the checkpoint make it worse?
How should the second feed be added?

debrief.title: One checkpoint, two queries
text: A checkpoint belongs to exactly one query. It records which offsets that query read and which batches reached the sink. Two queries can't share that record, and Delta refuses the write with DELTA_CONCURRENT_TRANSACTION.
The copied notebook also changed its source. Changing the number or type of sources generally needs a new checkpoint anyway.

debrief.title: Why not delete it
text: Deleting a checkpoint makes the next run start fresh: the record of what the original query had read and committed is gone, and with it the exactly-once guarantee for that history.
The error was the system protecting the data. The fix is to give the new query its own checkpoint, not to erase the old one's memory.

debrief.title: Adding the feed properly
text: Give the partner stream its own checkpoint path. In a declarative pipeline, the same design is two append flows into one streaming table, with checkpoint locations managed for you.
Keep checkpoints out of the table directories, or in a folder starting with an underscore, which VACUUM leaves alone.

takeaway: Each streaming query needs its own checkpoint; never share one.
Deleting a checkpoint resets what the query knows it has done.
DELTA_CONCURRENT_TRANSACTION points at a shared checkpoint.
content.honesty: If you haven't run Structured Streaming jobs, say so, and explain what a checkpoint holds and why it must not be shared. If you have recovered a stream, describe what you kept and what you reset.

debrief.title: Checklist

debrief.title: Copied notebooks

sayIt.question: A risky shortcut was nearly taken under time pressure. What do you do afterwards?

Make the safe path the easy path.
Share the lesson with other teams.

debrief.title: Prevention

points: Pause and ask what the fix changes and what it costs.
Keep one person deciding during the incident.
Choose the fix that removes the cause.
Verify recovery before closing.
Review afterwards without blame.

How do you confirm both streams are healthy?

debrief.title: Code

Leave the original stream's checkpoint untouched.

debrief.title: Health

sayIt.question: Explain what a streaming checkpoint is and how exactly-once writes into Delta work.
points: The checkpoint stores offsets, commits, state and the query ID.
Each query needs its own checkpoint; sharing one fails with DELTA_CONCURRENT_TRANSACTION.
Deleting a checkpoint makes the query start fresh.
The Delta sink records each batch as a transaction identifier and skips one already committed.

scenarios.title: The customer who moved twice
scenarios.outcome: Two address changes in one batch broke a MERGE, and the quick fix sometimes kept the older address.

content.bookmark: MERGE allows one source row per target row. Deduplicate the source by its sequence, newest last, or let AUTO CDC apply changes in order for you.

check.prompt: In a Delta MERGE, how many source rows may match one target row?
options: One; several matches fail the merge
Any number; the last one wins
Two: one to update and one to delete
check.why: Only one source row may match a given target row. Several matches fail with DELTA_MULTIPLE_SOURCE_ROW_MATCHING_TARGET_ROW_IN_MERGE, so deduplicate the source first.

check.prompt: When change events arrive out of order, what does AUTO CDC use to apply them in the right order?
options: The order rows appear in the batch
The time each file arrived
The SEQUENCE BY column
check.why: AUTO CDC takes keys and a sequencing column (SEQUENCE BY) and uses it to handle out-of-order events.

check.prompt: Which slowly changing dimension type keeps the history of every change?
options: Type 1
Type 2
Neither: AUTO CDC keeps only current values
check.why: SCD type 1 overwrites with no history; SCD type 2 keeps history, for all columns or chosen ones.

check.prompt: In MERGE ... WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT, what value do target columns the insert doesn't set get?
options: The value from the matching row in an earlier batch
NULL
The column's value in the previous target row
check.why: WHEN NOT MATCHED inserts the row; unspecified target columns get NULL.

caseStudy.setting: An insurer (fictional) receives change events from its policy system every hour: one row per change to a customer, with an event_time. A job MERGEs each hour's batch into silver.customers on customer_id, updating the address when matched and inserting when not.

events.what: A customer changes address twice within the hour. The MERGE fails with DELTA_MULTIPLE_SOURCE_ROW_MATCHING_TARGET_ROW_IN_MERGE.
An engineer adds dropDuplicates(["customer_id"]) to the source before the MERGE. The job succeeds.
Customer service finds letters going to old addresses. Some customers in silver have the earlier of two same-hour addresses, and one event that arrived late overwrote a newer address.

pipeline: Policy system · change events with customer_id, address, event_time
Hourly batch · one file of events, possibly several per customer
MERGE INTO silver.customers ON customer_id · WHEN MATCHED UPDATE, WHEN NOT MATCHED INSERT
tasks: Why did the first fix keep old addresses?
How should the changes be applied?

debrief.title: Why the MERGE failed
text: Two source rows matched the same target row. MERGE can't know which update to apply, so it refuses rather than guess. That refusal is the protection.

debrief.title: Why the quick fix was wrong
text: dropDuplicates on customer_id keeps one row per customer, but nothing in it chooses the newest event. Sometimes it kept the earlier address.
It also did nothing about events arriving late: a late, older event in a later batch matched the customer and overwrote the newer address, because the MERGE never compared event times.

debrief.title: Applying changes in order
text: By hand: keep the latest event per customer by event_time before the MERGE, and update only when the incoming event_time is newer than the stored one (a condition on WHEN MATCHED).

With declarative pipelines: AUTO CDC takes the key and SEQUENCE BY event_time and handles out-of-order events, as SCD type 1 (current address only) or type 2 (address history). It needs serverless pipelines or the Pro or Advanced edition.

takeaway: MERGE needs one source row per target row: deduplicate by sequence, not arbitrarily.
Compare event times so a late event can't overwrite a newer one.
AUTO CDC with SEQUENCE BY handles ordering, and SCD type 2 keeps history.

debrief.title: Acceptance test

Add tests for the cases that were missed.

debrief.title: MERGE or AUTO CDC

Check licences, editions and skills.
Consider what the business will need next.
Fix the immediate risk either way.
Decide with the people who will run it.

debrief.title: Hand-built
text: Keep the latest row per customer_id by event_time (a window with row_number, for example), then MERGE with WHEN MATCHED AND s.event_time > t.event_time THEN UPDATE and WHEN NOT MATCHED THEN INSERT.

debrief.title: AUTO CDC

sayIt.question: How do you apply a change data feed to a Delta table correctly?
points: MERGE needs one source row per target row; duplicates fail the merge.
Deduplicate by a sequence column, keeping the newest.
Compare sequence values so late events don't overwrite newer data.
AUTO CDC handles keys, SEQUENCE BY and out-of-order events.
Choose SCD type 1 for current values, type 2 for history.

scenario_levels.name: Tables you can trust
scenario_levels.about: History, recovery, deletion and layout: what Delta Lake keeps, what it removes, and what that means for audits and speed.

scenarios.title: The audit that asked for last month
scenarios.outcome: History listed the version the auditor wanted, but its data files had already been vacuumed, so the table could not be read as it was.

content.bookmark: Time travel needs a version's log entry and its data files. The log is kept 30 days by default; the files only 7 once VACUUM runs. History is not a backup.

check.prompt: What is the default for delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration, the threshold VACUUM uses?
options: 30 days
7 days
90 days
check.why: Data files no longer referenced are kept for 7 days by default; VACUUM removes them after that.

check.prompt: What is the default for delta.logRetentionDuration, how long table history is kept?
options: 30 days
7 days
365 days
check.why: History is kept for 30 days by default.

check.prompt: What do you need to time travel to a version?
options: Only its entry in DESCRIBE HISTORY, which is kept for 30 days
Only its data files; the log can be rebuilt from them
Both its log entry and its data files
check.why: A version is the log plus the files it points to. If VACUUM has removed the files, the version can't be read, even though history still lists it.

check.prompt: Predictive optimization runs VACUUM on a managed table whose deletedFileRetentionDuration is set to 2 days. How long are removed files kept?
options: 2 days, exactly as the property says
30 days, to match the log retention
At least 7 days
check.why: Predictive optimization honours the property but keeps at least 7 days even if it is set lower.

caseStudy.setting: A payments company (fictional) keeps daily settlement balances in a Unity Catalog managed table, updated by a nightly MERGE. Predictive optimization runs maintenance, including VACUUM, with default retention. Nobody has set any retention property.

events.what: An auditor asks for the balances exactly as they stood at month end, 20 days ago, to compare with a regulator's figures.
An analyst runs DESCRIBE HISTORY and finds the version from that night. SELECT ... TIMESTAMP AS OF that date fails: time travel to a version older than the file retention is blocked.
The finance director asks why the history shows the version if the data can't be read, and whether this can happen again.

pipeline: Nightly MERGE · updates settlement balances
finance.settlement.balances · managed Delta table, default retention
Predictive optimization · runs OPTIMIZE, VACUUM and ANALYZE automatically
tasks: Why does history list a version the table can't return?
What should the team change, and what can still be done for the auditor?

debrief.title: Two retentions
text: The log and the data files are kept for different times. History (the log) is kept 30 days by default, so the month-end version is listed. Removed data files are kept 7 days, then VACUUM deletes them.
Each nightly MERGE rewrote files, so the month-end version's files had been removed as no longer referenced. Without them the version can't be read, and recent runtimes block the attempt.

debrief.title: Changing the setting
text: For 30 days of time travel, set deletedFileRetentionDuration to 30 days to match the log. Longer retention costs storage.
With predictive optimization, raise the property before relying on it: its VACUUM honours the property and never keeps less than 7 days.

debrief.title: History isn't a backup
text: Databricks advises against using table history as a long-term backup. A month-end figure the business must reproduce belongs in a deliberate copy, such as a month-end snapshot table written by the job.
For the auditor now: if the source system or a downstream report kept month-end figures, reconstruct from those, and say plainly what can't be reproduced.

takeaway: Time travel needs both the log and the data files.
Raise deletedFileRetentionDuration if you need longer than 7 days.
Keep figures you must reproduce as deliberate snapshots, not as history.
content.honesty: If you haven't managed Delta retention, say so, and explain the two retentions and why VACUUM ends time travel. If you have answered an audit request from data history, describe what you could and couldn't reproduce.

points: Each write makes a new version; DESCRIBE HISTORY lists them.
Read old versions with VERSION AS OF or TIMESTAMP AS OF.

scenarios.title: The restore that doubled a report
scenarios.outcome: A RESTORE put silver right after a bad load, but gold, fed by a stream, kept the bad rows and the restore added to them.

content.bookmark: RESTORE is a data change: a stream reading the table can see it as new data. And restoring a source never removes what a streaming table already appended downstream.

check.prompt: Which privilege does RESTORE TABLE need?
options: SELECT
BROWSE
MODIFY
check.why: Restoring changes the table's data, so it needs MODIFY.

check.prompt: Why can a RESTORE cause duplicates downstream?
options: It is recorded as a data change, so a stream reading the table treats it as new data
It copies the table to a new location
It switches off the transaction log while it runs
check.why: RESTORE is a data-changing operation (dataChange=true). A streaming job reading the table sees it as new data and can produce duplicates downstream.

check.prompt: A streaming table has already appended some rows, and its source is then corrected. What happens to those rows?
options: They are recomputed at the next update, like every other row whose source changed
They stay as they are unless the table is fully refreshed
They are removed when the source is vacuumed
check.why: Rows a streaming table has already appended are not reprocessed; a full refresh clears the table and reprocesses the source.

check.prompt: Which kind of pipeline dataset stays correct when its source updates or deletes rows?
options: A view used only inside the pipeline
A streaming table
A materialized view
check.why: A materialized view is recomputed to match the source's current state, incrementally when possible; it suits sources that update or delete.

caseStudy.setting: A food-delivery company (fictional) keeps orders in silver.orders. A declarative pipeline reads silver.orders as a stream into a gold streaming table, revenue_events, which feeds a revenue dashboard.

events.what: A job is rerun by mistake and appends Wednesday's orders to silver a second time. The pipeline's next update appends them to gold too, and Wednesday's revenue doubles on the dashboard.
An engineer runs RESTORE TABLE silver.orders TO VERSION AS OF the version before the rerun. Silver is correct again.
The dashboard is still wrong. Gold still holds the duplicate orders, and after the restore some appear yet again.

pipeline: silver.orders · Delta table
Declarative pipeline · streaming read of silver.orders
gold.revenue_events · streaming table
Revenue dashboard · sums gold
tasks: Why didn't restoring silver fix gold?
How do they recover, and what should they do next time?

debrief.title: Why gold stayed wrong
text: A streaming table processes each source row once and doesn't reprocess rows it has already appended. Restoring silver changed silver, not the rows gold had already taken.
RESTORE is also recorded as a data change. To a stream reading silver, that commit can look like new data, which is how the restore added to gold instead of cleaning it.

debrief.title: Recovering
text: Run a full refresh of gold.revenue_events: the table is cleared, its checkpoints reset, and the now-correct silver reprocessed. Then check Wednesday's revenue against silver.
Weigh making revenue a materialized view, which is recomputed to match its source, so corrections in silver flow through without a full refresh.

debrief.title: Next time
text: Before restoring a table, find what reads it (lineage shows the downstream tables) and plan the step for each: a full refresh for streaming tables, nothing for materialized views.
Make the load safe to rerun, so a mistaken rerun doesn't duplicate data in the first place.

takeaway: RESTORE is a data change; streams reading the table can duplicate it.
Fixing a source doesn't fix what a streaming table already appended: full refresh it.
Plan the downstream step before you restore.

scenarios.title: Deleted, but still in the files
scenarios.outcome: A customer's erasure request was answered with a DELETE, but deletion vectors, history and the change feed still held the data on storage.

content.bookmark: DELETE hides rows from the current version. To remove them from storage: REORG TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE), then VACUUM once the retention has passed.

check.prompt: A table has deletion vectors enabled. What does DELETE do to the Parquet file holding the row?
options: Rewrites the Parquet file straight away, without the deleted row
Leaves the file and marks the row as deleted in metadata
Deletes the whole Parquet file and copies the other rows to a new one
check.why: With deletion vectors, the row is marked in metadata and readers apply the mark at query time; the file isn't rewritten.

check.prompt: Which sequence physically removes deleted rows from storage?
options: OPTIMIZE, then DESCRIBE HISTORY
VACUUM alone, straight after the DELETE
REORG TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE), then VACUUM once the retention has passed
check.why: REORG ... APPLY (PURGE) rewrites the files without the marked rows; VACUUM then deletes the old files once they are past the retention threshold.

check.prompt: Straight after the DELETE, can a reader still see the row?
options: Yes, by time travel to an earlier version, until its files are vacuumed
No, never
Only the table's owner can, because time travel needs ownership
check.why: Earlier versions keep their files until VACUUM removes them after the retention period, so time travel still returns the row.

check.prompt: Where are legacy change data feed files kept, and what removes them?
options: In _delta_log, removed by OPTIMIZE
In _change_data, removed by VACUUM
Nowhere: changes are only computed at read time
check.why: Legacy change data feed records changes on write in _change_data, which follows the table's retention and is removed by VACUUM.

caseStudy.setting: A fitness app (fictional) stores member profiles in a Delta table with deletion vectors enabled and legacy change data feed turned on, so a downstream system can pick up changes. A member asks for their personal data to be erased.

events.what: An engineer runs DELETE FROM members WHERE member_id = 4172 and confirms that a SELECT returns nothing. The request is marked complete.
The privacy officer asks whether the data is gone from storage, not just from queries. An engineer shows that SELECT ... VERSION AS OF the previous version still returns the member.
The team realises the change feed recorded the delete with the row's values, and that the table also had a column dropped last month under column mapping.

pipeline: members · Delta table, deletion vectors on, legacy change data feed on
DELETE · marks the row in a deletion vector
Downstream sync · reads the change feed
tasks: Where does the member's data still exist?
What steps actually remove it?

debrief.title: Where the data still is
text: In the current data files: with deletion vectors, the DELETE only marked the row; the Parquet file still contains it.
In older versions: earlier versions point to files holding the row, readable by time travel until VACUUM removes them.
In the change feed: legacy change data feed wrote change files under _change_data, which stay until VACUUM removes them.

debrief.title: Removing it
text: Run REORG TABLE members APPLY (PURGE) to rewrite the files without the marked rows. Then, once the retention threshold has passed, VACUUM removes the old files and the change files.
The dropped column is a soft delete too: under column mapping its data stays in the files until REORG TABLE and VACUUM.

debrief.title: Making it routine
text: The erasure procedure should state that it ends with REORG and VACUUM, and when the request counts as done: after the retention period, not after the DELETE.
Don't shorten retention below 7 days to speed this up: Databricks strongly recommends at least 7 days, because shorter retention can delete files that long-running jobs still need.

takeaway: DELETE hides rows; with deletion vectors the files still hold them.
REORG ... APPLY (PURGE), then VACUUM after the retention period, removes them.
History and change feed files hold the data until VACUUM.
content.honesty: If you haven't handled an erasure request on a lakehouse, say so, and explain the difference between a logical and a physical delete in Delta. If you have, describe how you proved the data was gone.

debrief.title: Done

debrief.title: Acceptance criteria

debrief.title: Timeline

debrief.title: Ownership

sayIt.question: How do you organise compliance work that spans several teams?
points: Name an owner for the outcome and for each step.
Write the procedure and its definition of done.
Track each request to completion with evidence.
Review the procedure when the platform changes.

tasks: What commands complete the erasure?
How do you verify it?

debrief.title: Commands
text: DELETE the rows; REORG TABLE members APPLY (PURGE); after the retention threshold, VACUUM members.

debrief.title: Verifying

sayIt.question: How do you physically delete personal data from a Delta table?
points: DELETE removes rows from the current version only.
With deletion vectors, rows are marked, not rewritten.
REORG TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE) rewrites files without them.
VACUUM then deletes old files, including change feed files, after the retention period.

scenarios.title: The column that stopped the stream
scenarios.outcome: An analyst added a column to a busy silver table at midday; the stream reading it stopped and a concurrent write failed.

content.bookmark: A schema change ends every stream reading the table and conflicts with concurrent writes. Make schema changes on purpose, at a planned time, with streams set to restart.

check.prompt: A stream reads a Delta table. Someone adds a column to that table. What happens to the stream?
options: Nothing: new columns are picked up silently
It stops and must be restarted
It switches to reading in batch
check.why: Updating a table's schema terminates any stream reading it; the stream must be restarted.

check.prompt: An INSERT writes an INT value into a BIGINT column. What happens?
options: It succeeds by a safe cast
It fails with a type mismatch
The value becomes NULL
check.why: Schema enforcement first tries a safe cast; an INT into a BIGINT column succeeds.

check.prompt: A write with mergeSchema adds a new column. Where does it go?
options: At the start of the table
In alphabetical order
At the end
check.why: Automatic schema evolution adds new columns at the end (or at the end of their struct), with their case preserved.

check.prompt: What lets you rename or drop a column without rewriting the data files?
options: OPTIMIZE FULL
Column mapping
A new streaming checkpoint
check.why: Renaming and dropping columns without a rewrite need column mapping enabled on the table.

caseStudy.setting: A telecoms company (fictional) keeps call records in silver.calls. A continuous job streams silver.calls into a gold aggregate, and an hourly job MERGEs late corrections into silver.calls.

events.what: An analyst who owns a report runs ALTER TABLE silver.calls ADD COLUMNS (roaming_flag BOOLEAN) to prepare for a new field.
The gold stream stops. The hourly MERGE, running at the same moment, fails with DELTA_METADATA_CHANGED.
The continuous job restarts the stream and it carries on; the MERGE succeeds on its next run. The analyst asks why a harmless column caused two failures.

pipeline: silver.calls · Delta table, written by an hourly MERGE
Continuous job · streams silver.calls into gold
ALTER TABLE ... ADD COLUMNS · run by hand
tasks: Why did adding a column cause two failures?
How should schema changes be made on this table?

debrief.title: Why two failures
text: Adding a column is a metadata change. A schema update terminates any stream reading the table, so the gold stream stopped and needed a restart.
Metadata changes also conflict with concurrent writes. The MERGE had read the table before the change and failed its commit with DELTA_METADATA_CHANGED instead of writing against an outdated schema.

debrief.title: Why it recovered
text: The stream ran in a continuous job, which starts a new run after a failure. Designing streams to restart automatically is Databricks' production advice for exactly these stops.
The MERGE succeeded on its next run because the conflict was a one-off. Retrying is the documented answer to a concurrent-modification error.

debrief.title: Making schema changes safely
text: Schedule schema and property changes away from writes, and have them made by the table's owners, ideally through the same deployment process as the pipeline code.
Often no hand-run ALTER is needed: a write with mergeSchema or MERGE WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION adds the column when data for it first arrives.

takeaway: A schema change terminates streams reading the table.
Metadata changes conflict with concurrent writes; retry them.
Plan schema changes; let streams restart automatically.
content.honesty: If you haven't changed the schema of a live Delta table, say so, and explain why it stops streams and conflicts with writes. If you have, describe how you scheduled it.

Automate where possible.

sayIt.question: Explain schema enforcement and evolution in Delta Lake.
points: Enforcement checks writes against the table's schema, trying safe casts first.

mergeSchema and WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION add new columns at the end.

scenarios.title: Ten thousand tiny files
scenarios.outcome: A table partitioned by a high-cardinality column and fed every minute became thousands of small files, and every query paid for it.

content.bookmark: Small files and the wrong partition key slow every read. Check DESCRIBE DETAIL, compact with OPTIMIZE, and prefer liquid clustering to partitioning.

check.prompt: Which command shows how many files a Delta table has?
options: DESCRIBE HISTORY
SHOW GRANTS
DESCRIBE DETAIL (numFiles)
check.why: DESCRIBE DETAIL returns one row of metadata, including numFiles and sizeInBytes: how to see the file count before and after OPTIMIZE.

check.prompt: Does OPTIMIZE change query results or disturb a stream reading the table?
options: No: it makes no data change
Yes: results change until the next VACUUM
It stops streams until they are restarted
check.why: OPTIMIZE rewrites files with no data change: readers get the same results, and a stream reading the table isn't affected.

check.prompt: What does Databricks recommend for new tables, instead of partitioning or Z-order?
options: Partitioning by more columns
Liquid clustering
Running VACUUM more often
check.why: Databricks recommends liquid clustering for all new tables; it replaces partitioning and ZORDER, and its keys can change without rewriting data.

check.prompt: How many clustering keys can a liquid-clustered table have?
options: One
Up to four
Up to 32
check.why: Up to four keys, chosen from the columns most used in filters.

caseStudy.setting: An ad-tech company (fictional) writes click events to a Delta table every minute from a stream. When the table was created, someone partitioned it by advertiser_id, which has tens of thousands of values, "so each advertiser's queries are fast".

events.what: Queries are fine. The table is small.
Dashboards that filter by date across all advertisers take minutes. DESCRIBE DETAIL shows a very large numFiles and a small average file size.
Someone proposes a bigger SQL warehouse. Someone else asks whether the table's layout is the real problem.

events.clicks · Delta table, PARTITIONED BY (advertiser_id)
Dashboards · filter mostly by event date, sometimes by advertiser
tasks: Why did reads get slow?
What would you change, and in what order?

debrief.title: Why reads got slow
text: Each micro-batch wrote small files into many advertiser partitions, so the file count grew by thousands a day. Every query had to list and open far more files than the data needed.

The partition key matched only some queries. Most dashboards filter by date, which the partitioning doesn't help at all. Too many partitions is one of the cases where Databricks recommends liquid clustering.

debrief.title: Fixing the layout
text: Compact first: OPTIMIZE rewrites small files into larger ones, with no data change, so it can run while the stream writes. Compare numFiles in DESCRIBE DETAIL before and after.

Then fix the design: move from partitioning to liquid clustering on the columns queries filter by, such as event_time and advertiser_id (cluster on the timestamp itself, not a date column derived from it). On recent runtimes, ALTER TABLE ... REPLACE PARTITIONED BY WITH CLUSTER BY converts a partitioned table, followed by OPTIMIZE.

debrief.title: Keeping it healthy
text: On a Unity Catalog managed table, predictive optimization runs OPTIMIZE for you; otherwise schedule it (every one or two hours for heavily updated tables). Auto compaction also compacts small files.
A bigger warehouse would have spent more money opening the same small files. Fix the layout before buying compute.

takeaway: Check numFiles in DESCRIBE DETAIL when reads slow down.
OPTIMIZE compacts small files without changing data.
Prefer liquid clustering on filter columns to high-cardinality partitions.

scenario_levels.about: Who can read what, what dropping a table really does, and the job behaviours that quietly duplicate or skip work.

scenarios.title: Granted SELECT, still denied
scenarios.outcome: A table owner granted SELECT and the analysts still couldn't read it; then someone asked for a DENY that Unity Catalog SQL doesn't have.

content.bookmark: Reading a table needs SELECT on it, USE SCHEMA on its schema and USE CATALOG on its catalog. Unity Catalog SQL has no DENY statement: access is what you grant.

check.prompt: Which privileges does a user need to read a table in Unity Catalog?
options: SELECT on the table, USE SCHEMA on its schema and USE CATALOG on its catalog
SELECT on the table only
USE CATALOG on the catalog only
check.why: Reading needs all three. USE CATALOG and USE SCHEMA grant no data themselves; they are boundaries the owners control.

check.prompt: SELECT is granted on a schema. Which tables does it cover?
options: Only the tables that exist at the moment the grant is made; later tables need their own grants
None, until each table is granted separately
Current and future tables and views in the schema
check.why: Privileges on a catalog or schema are inherited by current and future objects inside it.

check.prompt: How do you stop a group reading a table in Unity Catalog?
options: Run a DENY SELECT statement on the table for that group, which overrides any grant
Don't grant access, or REVOKE the grant that gives it
Grant the group only USE CATALOG, which overrides the SELECT granted on the table
check.why: Unity Catalog SQL has no DENY statement (DENY belongs to legacy Hive metastore table access control). Access comes only from grants, so remove the grant that gives it.

check.prompt: Which privilege lets users see that objects exist and request access, without reading data?
options: MODIFY
BROWSE
USE SCHEMA
check.why: BROWSE, granted on a catalog, shows what exists without giving data; Databricks recommends granting it to all account users.

caseStudy.setting: A bank's analytics team (fictional) needs a new table, risk.scores.daily, owned by the risk engineering group. The table's owner runs GRANT SELECT ON TABLE risk.scores.daily TO `analysts`.

events.what: Analysts query the table and get INSUFFICIENT_PERMISSIONS. The owner checks SHOW GRANTS: SELECT is there.
To "just make it work", someone proposes granting the analysts ALL PRIVILEGES on the whole risk catalog.

Table risk.scores.daily · SELECT granted to analysts

debrief.title: Why SELECT wasn't enough
text: Reading a table needs three privileges: SELECT on the table, USE SCHEMA on risk.scores and USE CATALOG on risk. The analysts had only the first.
The usage privileges grant no data. They let the catalog and schema owners control who can reach anything inside, which is why the table owner's grant alone can't open it.

debrief.title: What to grant
text: Grant USE CATALOG on risk and USE SCHEMA on risk.scores to analysts, keeping SELECT on the one table. ALL PRIVILEGES on the catalog would give far more than reading, including on every future object.
Remember inheritance: SELECT on the schema would cover every current and future table in it. Grant at schema level only if that is the intent.
Grant BROWSE on the catalog to all account users so people can find tables and request access.

debrief.title: Blocking the contractors
text: There is no DENY statement in Unity Catalog SQL; DENY statements belong to the legacy Hive metastore's table access control. Unity Catalog's only denial is an ABAC DENY policy, in Beta and limited to the MANAGE ACCESS CONTROL privilege.

So structure the groups: put contractors in their own group and grant the sensitive table only to a group without them. To hide some rows or columns rather than the whole table, use a row filter or column mask.

takeaway: Reading needs SELECT plus USE SCHEMA plus USE CATALOG.
Grants on a schema or catalog cover future objects too.
Unity Catalog SQL has no DENY: control access through grants and groups.

tasks: Which statements would you run?
How would you handle the contractors technically?

debrief.title: Statements
text: GRANT USE CATALOG ON CATALOG risk TO `analysts`; GRANT USE SCHEMA ON SCHEMA risk.scores TO `analysts`; keep GRANT SELECT ON TABLE risk.scores.daily TO `analysts`.

debrief.title: Contractors
text: Split the group: `analysts-staff` gets the sensitive table, `analysts-contractors` doesn't. Or a row filter or column mask using is_account_group_member().

sayIt.question: Explain how privileges work in Unity Catalog.
points: Users start with no access; owners and users with MANAGE grant privileges.
Reading needs SELECT, USE SCHEMA and USE CATALOG.

scenarios.title: Dropped the table, the files stayed
scenarios.outcome: A storage clean-up dropped external tables and saved nothing, while a managed table dropped by mistake was nearly given up for lost.

content.bookmark: Dropping an external table removes only its metadata; the files stay. Dropping a managed table deletes its files after a recovery period, and UNDROP TABLE brings it back within it.

check.prompt: What does DROP TABLE do to an external table?
options: Removes the metadata and leaves the files
Removes the metadata and the files
Moves the files into the schema's managed storage, so they are deleted later
check.why: Unity Catalog manages only an external table's metadata. Dropping it removes the metadata; the files stay at their path.

check.prompt: A managed table was dropped by mistake yesterday. How do you get it back?
options: Only from a storage backup
RESTORE TABLE to the version before the drop, which brings back its files and grants
UNDROP TABLE, within the recovery period (7 days by default)
check.why: Managed tables' files are deleted automatically after the recovery period ends; UNDROP TABLE recovers the table within it.

check.prompt: Are Unity Catalog privileges enforced when another tool reads an external table's files directly from storage?
options: Yes, always: the external location enforces the same privileges on every read
No: direct file access bypasses them
Only for SELECT
check.why: Unity Catalog privileges are not enforced on direct access to an external table's files.

check.prompt: Which converts an external Delta table to managed, keeping its name, permissions and history?
options: CREATE TABLE ... AS SELECT into a new table
ALTER TABLE t SET MANAGED
MSCK REPAIR TABLE t SYNC METADATA
check.why: ALTER TABLE ... SET MANAGED keeps the name, settings, permissions, views and history, and can be rolled back within 14 days. CTAS works too but loses these.

caseStudy.setting: A media company (fictional) moved to Unity Catalog last year. Early tables were created as external tables over ADLS paths; newer ones are managed. Finance asks the data team to cut storage costs.

events.what: An engineer drops forty old external tables that nobody queries. The tables disappear from Catalog Explorer.
The storage bill hasn't moved. The files are all still in the ADLS containers.
While tidying up, someone drops content.engagement, a managed table still in use, by mistake. The team starts planning to rebuild it from source over several days.

pipeline: ADLS Gen2 containers · external locations registered in Unity Catalog
Old external tables · metadata in Unity Catalog, files in ADLS
content.engagement · managed table in the schema's managed storage
tasks: Why didn't dropping the tables reduce the bill?
How do they get content.engagement back, and what should change?

debrief.title: Why the bill didn't move
text: Unity Catalog manages an external table's metadata, not its files. Dropping the forty tables removed their entries; the data stayed in ADLS, and so did the cost.
To reclaim the space, the files must be deleted at their paths by someone with rights on the storage, once the owners agree the data isn't needed.

debrief.title: Getting the managed table back
text: Dropping a managed table deletes its files only after the recovery period, 7 days by default. Within it, UNDROP TABLE content.engagement brings the table back. No rebuild is needed.
The period can be set per catalog or schema, to 0 or 7-30 days, with RETAIN DROPPED. Check it before relying on it.

debrief.title: What should change
text: Prefer managed tables: they are Databricks' recommended type, cost less to store and query, get predictive optimization, and clean up after a drop.

Convert the remaining external Delta tables with ALTER TABLE ... SET MANAGED where nothing outside Databricks reads their files. External tables still fit data other tools read directly, but remember Unity Catalog privileges don't apply to that direct access.

takeaway: Dropping an external table leaves its files.
UNDROP TABLE recovers a dropped managed table within the recovery period.
Prefer managed tables; convert external ones with SET MANAGED where you can.

debrief.title: The dropped table

External: files at a path in an external location; Unity Catalog manages only metadata.

scenarios.title: The repair that duplicated a batch
scenarios.outcome: A task failed after writing half its output, Repair ran it again from the start, and silver held part of the day twice.

content.bookmark: Repair reruns failed tasks from the beginning with the current settings, and doesn't make them idempotent. A task that appends can duplicate on repair; write with MERGE or overwrite.

check.prompt: What does Repair run in a failed multi-task job run?
options: Every task in the job again, in the original order, with the original settings
Only the unsuccessful tasks and their dependants
Only the first task
check.why: Repair reruns only the unsuccessful tasks and the tasks that depend on them.

check.prompt: Which job and task settings does a repair run use?
options: The current settings
The settings of the failed run
The job's original settings when it was created
check.why: Repair uses the current job and task settings, so you fix the problem first and then repair.

check.prompt: A task wrote part of its output, then failed. What does Repair do about the part already written?
options: It rolls back the failed attempt's partial write first, then reruns the task
It skips the rows already written
Nothing: the task restarts from the beginning and isn't made idempotent
check.why: Lakeflow Jobs doesn't make tasks idempotent. A repaired task restarts from the beginning, so an appending task can duplicate data.

check.prompt: Which Run if condition runs a clean-up task whatever happened upstream?
options: All succeeded
At least one failed
All done
check.why: All done runs the task regardless of upstream results, which suits clean-up.

caseStudy.setting: An airline (fictional) runs a nightly job with three tasks: ingest bookings, transform them into silver, and publish a gold summary. The transform task processes each day's bookings in several steps, appending each step's output to silver.bookings.

events.what: Transform appends the first three steps' output, then fails on a bad date format. Publish is marked Upstream failed.
An engineer fixes the date parsing in the notebook and clicks Repair run. Transform and publish succeed.
Revenue analysts find that some of the day's bookings appear twice in silver and in the gold summary.

pipeline: Task 1 ingest · loads raw bookings into bronze
Task 2 transform · several steps, each appending to silver.bookings
Task 3 publish · builds the gold summary from silver
tasks: Why did the repair create duplicates?
How should the transform task write?

debrief.title: Why the repair duplicated
text: Repair did exactly what it says: it reran the failed transform task and its dependant, from the beginning, with the fixed code. The rows the failed attempt had already appended were still in silver.
Lakeflow Jobs doesn't make tasks idempotent. A task that appends will append again on repair.

debrief.title: Writing so reruns are safe
text: Make the transform's writes idempotent. Overwrite the day's slice, or MERGE on a booking key so a rerun updates rows instead of adding them. An insert-only MERGE on a unique key appends only rows that aren't already there.
Then Repair, Run now and retries are all safe, which is what a nightly job needs.

debrief.title: Cleaning up and the repair itself
text: Remove the duplicates for that day (rerun the day's transform with overwrite once it is idempotent), then let publish rebuild gold.
Repair was the right tool, used after the fix, because it uses the current settings. It only needs the tasks themselves to be safe to rerun.

takeaway: Repair reruns failed tasks from the start with current settings.
Jobs don't make tasks idempotent: design writes to be rerun safely.
Overwrite a slice or MERGE on a key instead of appending.

debrief.title: Existing jobs

text: Build the day's output, then MERGE INTO silver.bookings ON booking_id (update when matched, insert when not), or overwrite that day's rows in one write.

debrief.title: Clean-up

Tasks must be idempotent: overwrite or MERGE, not append.

scenarios.title: The stream that was down while the job was green
scenarios.outcome: One of three streams in a continuous job failed and stayed down for days; the job looked healthy and nobody was told.

content.bookmark: In a job with several continuous tasks, a failed task retries on its own only with Task retry mode On failure. Notify on task failures, or give each critical stream its own job.

check.prompt: A continuous job runs several streaming tasks. When does a failed task retry on its own?
options: Always, immediately
Never: one failed task always means the whole job must be restarted by hand
Only if Task retry mode is set to On failure
check.why: With several continuous tasks, a failed task retries alone only with Task retry mode On failure; otherwise the job waits for all tasks to fail.

check.prompt: Are job-level notifications sent for tasks that are retried?
options: No: use task notifications to hear about every failure
Yes: job-level notifications are sent for every failed attempt of every task
Only when the retry also fails
check.why: Job-level notifications aren't sent for retried tasks; task notifications report every failure.

check.prompt: Why shouldn't a streaming job call awaitTermination()?
options: It deletes the checkpoint when the query ends
The Jobs service already keeps the run alive, and the call blocks the tracking that backlog notifications need
It doubles the DBUs billed
check.why: Use awaitTermination() only interactively or locally. In jobs it is unnecessary and blocks tracking.

check.prompt: How does a streaming backlog notification measure the backlog?
options: Once a day, as a summary of how far each stream fell behind
On every micro-batch
As a 10-minute average, repeating every 30 minutes while over the threshold
check.why: Streaming backlog alerts use a 10-minute average and repeat every 30 minutes.

caseStudy.setting: A ride-hailing company (fictional) runs one continuous Lakeflow job with three streaming tasks: trips, payments and driver locations. A failure notification is set on the job. Task retry mode was left at its setting from when the job was created.

events.what: The payments stream fails on a malformed record. The trips and locations streams keep running.
The job page shows the job running. No notification arrives. Payment dashboards show nothing new since Friday.
Finance escalates. An engineer finds the payments task failed on Friday and never ran again.

pipeline: Continuous job · three streaming tasks: trips, payments, locations
Job-level failure notification · email to the data team
Task retry mode · not set to On failure
tasks: Why did the payments stream stay down with no alert?
How should the job be set up?

debrief.title: Why it stayed down
text: With several continuous tasks in one job, a failed task retries on its own only when Task retry mode is On failure. Otherwise the job waits for all tasks to fail, so one dead stream can stay down while the job looks healthy.
The job never failed as a whole, so the job-level notification had nothing to report.

debrief.title: Setting it up
text: Set Task retry mode to On failure, and add task-level failure notifications so every failure reaches someone. Or give each critical stream its own job.
Add a streaming backlog notification on payments: it would have fired once unprocessed data passed its threshold, hours into Friday evening rather than on Monday.

debrief.title: The malformed record
text: A retry would fail on the same record again. The stream also needs a way to handle bad input, such as an expectation that drops or quarantines invalid rows, so one record can't stop the stream.
Make sure the code doesn't call awaitTermination(), which blocks the tracking backlog notifications use.

takeaway: Several streams in one job need Task retry mode On failure.
Use task notifications; job-level ones miss task retries.
Alert on streaming backlog, not only on failure.

Report reliability to stakeholders.

text: Task retry mode On failure; task-level failure notifications; a streaming backlog threshold on each stream; or separate jobs per critical stream.

debrief.title: Bad records

sayIt.question: How do you run Structured Streaming reliably in production?
points: Run streams as Lakeflow jobs or pipelines on jobs compute, never all-purpose compute.
Configure automatic restart; the continuous trigger retries with exponential backoff.
With several streams in a job, use Task retry mode On failure.
Use task notifications and streaming backlog alerts.
Don't call awaitTermination() in jobs.

scenarios.title: The mask on every table but one
scenarios.outcome: Column masks were set by hand table by table; a new table with customer emails went out without one, and its files were also readable outside Unity Catalog.

content.bookmark: Masks and filters set one table at a time are only as good as the last table someone remembered. ABAC policies on governed tags cover new tagged tables automatically.

check.prompt: What is a column mask in Unity Catalog?
options: A SQL UDF that returns the real value or a masked one for each query
A copy of the table with the column removed
A privilege that hides the column from SHOW GRANTS
check.why: A column mask is a SQL UDF applied to a column at query time; it returns the value or a masked version, often based on is_account_group_member().

check.prompt: What does Databricks recommend for applying masks and filters consistently across many tables?
options: A column mask set on each table by its owner
Dynamic views over every table
ABAC policies using governed tags
check.why: ABAC policies attached to a catalog, schema or table, matched by governed tags, are Databricks' recommended approach for consistency; new tables with the tag are covered automatically.

check.prompt: An ABAC policy is attached to a catalog. Can a table owner inside it override the policy?
options: Yes: a table owner can drop the policy's mask on their own table at any time
No: table owners can't override the policy
Only by setting a stronger mask
check.why: Policies apply to matching tables in their scope, and table owners can't override them.

check.prompt: An external table's files are read directly from storage by another tool. Do its Unity Catalog masks apply?
options: Yes, masks travel with the files
Only for the columns that carry a governed tag, because tags are stored in the files
No: Unity Catalog privileges aren't enforced on direct file access
check.why: Direct access to an external table's files bypasses Unity Catalog, so neither grants nor masks apply.

caseStudy.setting: An online retailer (fictional) masks customer email addresses for everyone outside customer support. Each table owner adds a column mask by hand with ALTER TABLE ... ALTER COLUMN email SET MASK. A new marketing table, marketing.campaigns.recipients, is created as an external table so an outside email tool can read its files.

A privacy review finds the unmasked column. The owner adds the mask. The reviewer then asks what the outside email tool can see.
The answer is everything: the tool reads the Parquet files directly from storage, where Unity Catalog masks don't apply.

marketing.campaigns.recipients · external table, no mask at first
Outside email tool · reads the table's files directly from ADLS
tasks: Why was the new table unprotected?

debrief.title: Why the table was unprotected
text: Table-level masks are set by the table owner, one table at a time. The rule "emails are masked" lived in people's memory, and the new table's owner didn't know it.

Databricks recommends ABAC policies for consistency across many tables: tag the column with a governed tag (for example PII), and attach a column-mask policy to the catalog. Any new table whose column carries the tag is covered, and owners can't override it.

debrief.title: The outside tool
text: Unity Catalog's controls apply to queries through Databricks. Direct reads of an external table's files bypass them, masks included.
Give the tool only what it should see: write the recipients it needs, without the fields it mustn't have, to the location it reads, or have it query through Databricks so the policies apply.

debrief.title: Choosing the tools
text: Row filters and column masks protect one table. ABAC policies with governed tags protect every matching table. Dynamic views expose a curated slice to people without access to the base tables.
Keep mask functions simple and deterministic: Databricks' performance advice favours simple SQL UDFs with few arguments.

takeaway: Per-table masks depend on someone remembering each table.
ABAC policies with governed tags cover new tagged tables automatically.
Direct file access to external tables bypasses Unity Catalog's controls.

scenarios.title: The all-purpose bill
scenarios.outcome: Production jobs ran on an all-purpose cluster that never shut down, and the first monthly bill was several times the estimate.

content.bookmark: All-purpose compute is for interactive work and is billed at a different rate from jobs compute. Automated work belongs on jobs compute or serverless, and idle compute should terminate.

check.prompt: On Azure, what counts as a Jobs Compute workload for billing?
options: Any job, whatever cluster it uses
A job that both starts and terminates the cluster it runs on
Any cluster, all-purpose or not, with fewer than ten workers at the time of the run
check.why: The Azure pricing page defines Jobs Compute as a job that both starts and terminates its cluster; other work, such as notebook commands, is all-purpose and billed at a different rate.

check.prompt: For classic compute, what does Azure Databricks bill?
options: The virtual machines provisioned plus DBUs
DBUs only
A flat monthly fee per workspace, whatever compute runs in it
check.why: Azure Databricks bills for the VMs in clusters and for DBUs based on the VM type. For serverless, compute is in Databricks' account, so only DBUs are billed.

check.prompt: Which system table holds billable usage in DBUs?
options: system.access.audit
system.query.history
system.billing.usage
check.why: system.billing.usage records all billable usage in DBUs; joined with prices and compute tables, it attributes spend to jobs and warehouses.

check.prompt: Which control lets admins limit cluster size and cost per cluster?
options: Secret scopes
Compute policies
Git folders
check.why: Compute policies limit what users can create: fixed or hidden settings, cluster counts, maximum cost per cluster.

caseStudy.setting: A healthcare analytics start-up (fictional) moves its nightly pipelines to Azure Databricks. To move fast, the team creates one large all-purpose cluster with autoscaling, attaches every job to it, and switches off automatic termination "so jobs never wait for start-up".

events.what: Everything works. The cluster also hosts the team's daytime notebooks.
The first bill is several times the estimate. The cluster ran all month, and all of its work was billed at the all-purpose rate.
The CFO asks which jobs cost what, and what can be cut without slowing the pipelines.

pipeline: One all-purpose cluster · autoscaling, auto termination off
Nightly jobs · attached to the all-purpose cluster
Daytime notebooks · same cluster
tasks: Why was the bill so high?
What would you change, and how would you show the CFO where the money goes?

debrief.title: Why the bill was high
text: Two things. The cluster never shut down, so VMs and DBUs were billed every hour of the month, including idle nights and weekends.

And on Azure, Jobs Compute means a job that starts and terminates its own cluster. Jobs run on a shared all-purpose cluster are all-purpose work, billed at a different rate. Databricks doesn't recommend all-purpose compute for production jobs.

debrief.title: What to change
text: Run each job on jobs compute (a cluster the job starts and stops) or on serverless jobs compute, Databricks' recommended compute for notebook and Python tasks, which starts fast and leaves minimal idle time.

Keep a smaller all-purpose cluster for daytime notebooks, with automatic termination after a set number of idle minutes. Use compute policies to cap size and enforce termination, and tag compute so usage can be attributed.

debrief.title: Showing where the money goes
text: Query system.billing.usage: usage in DBUs by date, SKU and job (usage_metadata.job_id), joined with system.billing.list_prices to estimate cost. Records usually appear within 12 hours.
Report spend per job and per team from tags, and review it monthly.

takeaway: All-purpose compute isn't for production jobs.

scenarios.title: One task ran for an hour
scenarios.outcome: A daily aggregation stalled on one task for one huge customer; more workers changed nothing, because adaptive query execution doesn't split a skewed groupBy.

content.bookmark: When one task takes far longer than the rest, it's skew. AQE splits skewed partitions in joins, not in aggregations; salt the hot key and aggregate in two stages.

check.prompt: In a stage's Summary Metrics, what signals skew?
options: Many tasks of similar length
The max task duration is 50% or more above the 75th percentile
Spill on every task in the stage, whatever the task durations
check.why: Databricks' guide: skew shows as a max task duration 50% or more above the 75th percentile.

check.prompt: Does adaptive query execution split a skewed partition in a groupBy aggregation?
options: No: it splits skewed partitions in sort-merge and shuffle-hash joins
Yes, automatically
Only when Photon is enabled on the cluster running the query
check.why: AQE's skew handling applies to sort-merge and shuffle-hash joins. A skewed aggregation needs another fix, such as salting.

check.prompt: What is salting a key?
options: Encrypting the key before the shuffle
Caching the hot key's rows on every worker
Adding a random value to the hot key so its rows spread over many tasks, then aggregating in two stages
check.why: Salting splits one hot key into several, so the first aggregation runs in parallel; a second aggregation combines the partial results.

check.prompt: What is spill in the Spark UI?
options: Rows dropped because they didn't fit in the executor's memory
Execution memory ran out, so data was written to disk
Network traffic between executors
check.why: Spill means execution memory was exhausted and data was written to disk; it is most common in shuffles.

caseStudy.setting: A marketplace (fictional) computes daily sales per seller with a groupBy on seller_id over billions of order lines. One seller, a large retailer that joined last month, accounts for a large share of all orders.

events.what: The daily job goes from 10 minutes to over an hour. In the Spark UI, one stage has hundreds of tasks finishing in seconds and one task running for most of the hour.
The team doubles the number of workers. The job takes just as long.
Someone points out that AQE is on by default and asks why it isn't fixing this.

pipeline: silver.order_lines · billions of rows
groupBy("seller_id").agg(sum("amount"))
gold.daily_seller_sales
tasks: Why didn't more workers help?
How would you fix it?

debrief.title: Why more workers didn't help
text: A groupBy shuffles so that all rows for one seller end up in one partition, processed by one task. The big seller's rows all went to that one task.

Adding workers adds tasks running in parallel, but that one task still had to process all the big seller's rows alone. The Summary Metrics showed it: a max task duration far above the 75th percentile.

debrief.title: Why AQE didn't fix it
text: AQE is on by default and does split skewed partitions, but in sort-merge and shuffle-hash joins. This was an aggregation, which its skew handling doesn't cover.
Databricks' guide lists salting for this case: add a salt to the hot key and aggregate in two stages.

debrief.title: The fix
text: Add a random salt (say 0-31) to each row, group by seller_id and salt to get partial sums spread over many tasks, then group the partial sums by seller_id. The big seller's work is shared by 32 tasks.

Other options from the same guide: liquid clustering when a stored table is skewed, and the REBALANCE hint when the output is skewed. Check spill too: if the slow task also spills, fewer rows per task helps both.

takeaway: Skew shows as one task far slower than the rest.
AQE splits skewed join partitions, not skewed aggregations.
Salt the hot key and aggregate in two stages.

scenarios.title: The 403 from serverless
scenarios.outcome: Classic clusters could read the firewalled storage account and serverless couldn't; the old way of allowing serverless had stopped working.

content.bookmark: Serverless compute runs in Databricks' account, not your VNet. To reach a firewalled storage account, allow the AzureDatabricksServerless service tag through a network security perimeter, or add a private endpoint in an NCC.

check.prompt: Where does serverless compute run in Azure Databricks?
options: In the workspace's injected VNet, next to the classic clusters in your subscription
In a serverless compute plane in the Azure Databricks account, in the workspace's region
In the control plane's web application
check.why: Classic compute runs in your subscription's VNet; serverless runs in a serverless compute plane in the Azure Databricks account, in the workspace's region.

check.prompt: What is a network connectivity configuration (NCC)?
options: An account-level, regional construct that manages private endpoints for serverless compute
A per-cluster setting for classic compute
A storage account firewall rule
check.why: An NCC is created by account admins, is regional, can be attached to up to 50 workspaces in the region, and manages serverless private endpoints.

check.prompt: A private endpoint is added in an NCC for a storage account. What has to happen before it works?
options: Nothing: it is active at once
Databricks support approves it after a review of the storage account
The storage account's owner accepts the request
check.why: Adding a private endpoint creates a request the resource owner must accept.

check.prompt: Does allowing serverless through a storage firewall also allow classic compute?
options: No: classic compute must be allowed separately
Yes, both use the same rule
Only when secure cluster connectivity is enabled on the workspace
check.why: A storage firewall affects classic compute too, and classic compute must be allowed separately.

debrief.title: Why classic worked and serverless didn't
text: Classic compute runs in the workspace's own VNet, whose subnets the firewall allows. Serverless runs in Databricks' account, outside that VNet, so the subnet rule doesn't cover it.
The rule meant for serverless allow-listed serverless subnet IDs, and the docs say such storage accounts can no longer connect. Without a supported rule, serverless gets 403 Forbidden.

debrief.title: Supported options
text: Network security perimeter: put the storage account in a perimeter and allow the AzureDatabricksServerless service tag, which can be scoped to a region.

Private endpoint: an account admin creates an NCC in the region, adds a private endpoint rule for the storage account, the storage owner accepts it, and the NCC is attached to the workspace. It needs the Premium plan.
Either way, keep the classic subnets allowed separately: a storage firewall applies to both kinds of compute.

debrief.title: Choosing
text: A private endpoint keeps the traffic private but adds limits to plan for (NCCs per region, endpoints per region) and a networking charge for serverless traffic to customer resources. The service tag is simpler to run.
Make the choice part of the platform's network design, so the next serverless workload doesn't rediscover the problem.

takeaway: Serverless isn't in your VNet: firewall rules for your subnets don't cover it.
Allowing serverless subnet IDs no longer works; use a network security perimeter or an NCC private endpoint.
Allow classic and serverless compute separately.

scenarios.title: The replica that copied the damage
scenarios.outcome: The disaster recovery plan replicated storage to another region, so when a bad job corrupted a table, the replica was corrupted too.

content.bookmark: Disaster recovery protects against losing a region, not against bad data: corruption replicates. Recover bad data with time travel or backups; replicate managed tables with Deep Clone.

check.prompt: Does a disaster recovery solution protect against data corruption?
options: Yes: the secondary region always keeps a clean copy from before the error
No: corrupted data replicates; use time travel or backups
Only with an active-active design
check.why: Databricks' guidance: a DR solution does not mitigate data corruption, because corrupted data replicates. Use time travel or backups for that.

check.prompt: How does Databricks recommend replicating managed table data to a DR region?
options: Rely on geo-redundant storage of the workspace's root storage
Copy only the _delta_log directory
Deep Clone
check.why: Replicate managed table data with Deep Clone, not by relying on geo-redundant storage of the workspace root storage.

check.prompt: What does RPO measure?
options: How much data loss is tolerated
How long restoring service may take
How many regions are in use
check.why: RPO is the data loss tolerated; RTO is the time to restore. Both are business decisions.

check.prompt: What is high availability within one region?
options: A secondary workspace in another region
Zone redundancy inside the region
Nightly backups to another subscription
check.why: HA is zone redundancy inside a region; DR is a secondary workspace in another region.

caseStudy.setting: An insurer (fictional) runs its claims platform on Azure Databricks. The DR plan, written early, says "storage is geo-redundant, so data is safe in the paired region". No one has tested a restore.

events.what: A faulty release of a nightly job overwrites claim statuses in a core managed table with wrong values.
Someone suggests failing over to the DR region. The replica has the same wrong statuses: the corruption replicated overnight.
The table is recovered with RESTORE from Monday's version, which is within the retention period. The board asks whether the DR plan protects anything at all.

Storage · geo-redundant replication to the paired region
DR plan · no secondary workspace, no tested restore
tasks: Why didn't the DR plan help?

debrief.title: Why DR didn't help
text: Replication copies whatever is written, including bad writes. Databricks says it plainly: a DR solution does not mitigate data corruption.
What saved the day was time travel: RESTORE to Monday's version worked because the files were still within the retention period.

debrief.title: Two different protections
text: For bad data: time travel and RESTORE within retention, with retention set long enough for how quickly the business notices errors, and backups for longer needs.

For losing a region: a secondary workspace in another region with replicated data and configuration. Databricks recommends its managed disaster recovery, and replicating managed tables with Deep Clone rather than relying on geo-redundant root storage. Active-passive is the common pattern.

debrief.title: What the plan needs
text: RPO and RTO agreed with the business per system, not assumed by engineers.
A tested failover and a tested restore, done on a schedule. A restore also needs its downstream effects handled, since RESTORE is a data change that streams reading the table can see as new data.

takeaway: DR covers losing a region; it doesn't undo bad data.
Time travel and backups recover corruption; set retention to match.
Agree RPO and RTO with the business, and test both recoveries.
